title: Void Linux Maintainer Orphans 100 Packages over AI Policy Dispute
content:
Void Linux Maintainer Orphans 100+ Packages Over AI Policy Dispute
A Void Linux maintainer has orphaned more than 100 packages he maintained over a dispute of the project's AI policy for LLM-generated text.
Void Linux contributor Andrea Brancaleoni last week submitted a Void package update for Go 1.27.1. As a follow-up to it, yesterday was this commit he posted referring to the results comparing the Go 1.26 to 1.27 package upgrade impact.
Another Void Linux maintainer then asked what was used in generating this text for comparison, to which Brancaleoni noted was GLM-5.3-Flash + OpenCode.
But the Void Linux project does have a contributing policy over AI usage that reads:
"In this section, "AI" refers to generative artificial intelligence tools, including Large Language Models and similar technologies.
So technically the policy was broken by using AI to generate comments on comments for that Void Linux pull request. And the usage of AI tools wasn't disclosed upfront in that offending message.
Now in turn, Brancaleoni decided to disown maintained packages that he oversees. That has resulted in 113 of the Void Linux packages set to be orphaned.
The now orphaned packages include Adapta, Autodia, SFML, abootimg, alacritty, arpwatch, asus-kbd-backlight, backblaze-b2, bash-preexec, beep, binfmt-support, bitlbee-facebook, bitlbee-steam, cdm, clementine, crane, csound, daemonize, darkhttpd, dep, diff-pdf, docker-cli, docker-gc, docker-gen, dtc, embree, entr, etcd, fcron, flannel, flint, font-fontin, forego, freeplane, fscrypt, gede, gettext-stub, git-cola, gkill, glock, go-bindata, go-jira, hans, hivex, hopper, hostaliases, hugo, iio-sensor-proxy, indicator-doom-cpu, interbench, ispc, jbigkit, kaitai-struct-compiler, kubernetes, kvirc, libguestfs, libnfc, libpodofo0.9.7, logstalgia, massren, mbox, mfoc, mkinitcpio-nfs-utils, mksh, moby, motion, openresolv, packer, pd, perl-Template-Toolkit, pinktrace, podofo, python3-Arrow, python3-b2sdk, python3-pdm-backend, python3-xattr, racket, rakarrack, rancher-compose, rmlint, rng-tools, rocker, runit-swap, sassc, scanmem, schroot, sift, splix, sublime-text3, subtle, supermin, sydbox, tag, tbb, terraform, terragrunt, texmaker, thermald, trollock, ttf-ubuntu-font-family, urbanterror-data, urbanterror, usbredir, vagrant, vba-m, virt-manager, virtme, webcat, websocketd, wpa_actiond, xboxdrv, xcompmgr, and yoshimi.
That includes some notable packages such as Alacritty, binfmt-support, Clementine, various Docker packages, fscrypt, Kubernetes, various Python 3 packages, and Intel Thermald now set to be orphaned unless other Void Linux maintainers step up to maintain them over this AI policy dispute.

report.summary: A Void Linux maintainer orphaned 113 packages after an AI-disclosure dispute over LLM-generated pull request text.
report.background: Void Linux is an independent, rolling-release, systemd-free distribution maintained entirely by volunteers, so each individual maintainer carries outsized weight. Across open source, projects from Curl and Gentoo to NetBSD and QEMU have spent the past two years arguing over AI-generated contributions: how much LLM text is acceptable, whether it must be disclosed, and who bears the review burden. Void's own policy is among the stricter ones — it requires that all content originate from and be understood by a human contributor, mandates disclosure of any AI tool use, and bans AI review tools from pull requests, while permitting AI translation. That backdrop turned a routine Go package bump into a test case for enforcing the rules.
key_points: The dispute began with a routine update: Andrea Brancaleoni bumped Void's Go package to 1.27.1 and posted a comparison of the 1.26-to-1.27 upgrade impact. When another maintainer asked what produced the text, he answered GLM-5.3-Flash plus OpenCode. Because the AI use was not disclosed up front, the post ran afoul of Void's contributing policy on AI-generated content.

Rather than retract the message or re-litigate the exchange, Brancaleoni disowned his maintainership of 113 packages, orphaning them. Orphaning is not deletion: it flags packages as lacking an owner so other maintainers can adopt them. But until someone does, those packages receive no routine version bumps, security fixes, or build repairs — a real regression risk on a rolling-release distro.

The casualty list is unusually high-profile for one maintainer's exit: Kubernetes, Docker-adjacent packages (moby, docker-cli, docker-gen, docker-gc), Terraform, Packer, Vagrant, rancher-compose, the Alacritty terminal, Hugo, Racket, Clementine, fscrypt, virt-manager, thermald, plus multiple Python and Perl libraries. DevOps and container tooling are especially hard hit.

Void's policy states that all contributions must be made by humans and understood by the contributor, covering code, documentation, issues, security reports, PR descriptions and comments. All AI tool usage must be disclosed, AI review tools are barred from pull requests, and only AI-powered human-language translation is explicitly permitted — a strict line compared with projects that merely ask for transparency.

The episode exposes a governance gap: policies can define acceptable AI use, but rarely specify proportionate consequences when a volunteer maintainer breaks them. Losing a contributor who handles over a hundred packages over a comment-generation technicality looks disproportionate to many observers, yet letting disclosure rules slide erodes trust. Neither outcome is comfortable for volunteer-run projects.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a disclosure-and-governance story rather than a capability one: it shows that vendors shipping capable coding agents into open source will keep colliding with community norms about authorship and reviewer workload. For developers, it sharpens the trade-off between AI-assisted speed and reputational risk — quietly using an agent and being caught can cost standing. For maintainers, it adds a policing duty few volunteered for. For regular users, the practical fallout is stale packages: Void users relying on Kubernetes, Docker, Terraform or Alacritty may see delayed updates and security patches until adopters step forward, and other distributions are watching how the dispute resolves.
report.tools: To follow up: OpenCode, the terminal AI coding agent named in the dispute, and the GLM model family; comparable agents include Aider, Claude Code and Cline. For policy comparison, read the AI contribution guidelines of Curl, Gentoo and Fedora. To help, check Void's orphaned-package list and adoption process, and project-health trackers such as Repology or distro watch dashboards for spotting unmaintained packages.
